paras: The killing of Louis Gibson was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Augusta, Georgia, policeman W. M. Belding on the night of August 25, 1900, during an attempted arrest. A coroner's jury found the next day that the killing was justifiable homicide. Two Georgia papers carried brief Augusta dispatches that presented the officer's account and described Gibson as a "desperate negro character."

According to the dispatches, Belding heard a woman's cries from the rear of a building and found Gibson beating his wife. In the officer's account, Gibson refused to submit to arrest, and in the struggle that followed he threw Belding to the ground and took his club. Belding then drew his pistol and fired, and the bullet struck Gibson just above the right ear and killed him instantly.

On August 26 the coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide, finding that Gibson had resisted arrest, seized the policeman's club and assaulted the officer. No report of further proceedings, of an account from Gibson's wife or other witnesses, or of any community response appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News printed its Augusta dispatch on August 27 under the headline "SUSTAINED THE POLICEMAN," sharing the item with the death of an Augusta cotton factor. Its account described a "terrible struggle" and gave the verdict as the news, with Belding's version stated as fact. A day later the Americus Times-Recorder ran a separately worded dispatch headlined "POLICEMAN KILLS A NEGRO," with the deck "Officer Sends a Bullet Through Desperado's Brain." That version called Gibson "a desperate negro character" who was "powerfully built," details absent from the Savannah report.
No coverage of the killing was found in the Black press or in an Augusta paper.

reader.title: Killing of Louis Gibson
bases: A city policeman shot and killed Louis Gibson while trying to arrest him, with no crowd involved (A1, A2).

Two separately worded Augusta dispatches agree that Policeman Belding shot and killed Gibson and that a coroner's jury found the killing justifiable, though both give only the officer's account of the struggle (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Officer's account as accepted by the coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Belding answered a woman's cries, found Gibson beating his wife, and shot him after Gibson resisted arrest, threw him to the ground and took his club.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headed its Augusta dispatch 'SUSTAINED THE POLICEMAN' and described a 'terrible struggle' before the shooting.
The Americus Times-Recorder headlined 'POLICEMAN KILLS A NEGRO' with the deck 'Officer Sends a Bullet Through Desperado's Brain' and called Gibson 'a desperate negro character'.

versions.value: 'Last night' in a dispatch dated August 26, i.e. the night of August 25
Dispatch dated August 27 with no shooting date given

conflicts.note: The two do not truly conflict; the Savannah dispatch is the only one that dates the shooting, and it places the inquest on August 26.

record_check.dossier: 1900-08-25 (night): the Augusta dispatch dated August 26 says Gibson was shot 'last night'; August 27 is only a later dispatch date.
Resisted arrest, seized the officer's club and assaulted him (officer's account, accepted by the coroner's jury)

sources.note: Augusta dispatch, Aug. 26: coroner's jury returns justifiable homicide for Policeman W. M. Belding, who shot Louis Gibson 'last night'; officer's account of resistance and seized club.
